name: Arequipa-La Unión Quechua
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

earlier_scan.note: no variety-specific description found (only classification refs Landerman 1991, Adelaar & Muysken 2004); generic Quechua penultimate stress NOT assumed per rules

new_statements.quote: The Quechua spoken in Arequipa belongs to the Cuzco-Bolivia variety. Unfortunately, the literature describing Arequipa Quechua is very scant, indeed [...] Quechua is an agglutinative language, with morphologically complex words constructed exclusively through suffixation. Each suffix usually consists of one or two syllables corresponding to a single morpheme, with word stress on the penultimate syllable. [p. 58:] Since these suffixes [the evidential enclitics -mi/-n, -chá, -cha, -s(i), -chu] always occur in word-final position, none but "Speculative" /-chá/ is ever phonologically stressed.
new_statements.citation: Courtney, Ellen Hazlehurst. 1998. Child Acquisition of Quechua Morphosyntax. PhD dissertation, University of Arizona. (Ch. 5 'The Quechua Language')
new_statements.locator: p. 47 (pdf p. 52); enclitic exception p. 58 (pdf p. 63); restated pp. 89, 91, 240
new_statements.check: confirmed by a second reader, with minor differences
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: FILE / The quotation was checked again. (333 pp, text layer). pdf p. 52 = printed p. 47, ch. 5 'The Quechua Language': "The Quechua spoken in Arequipa belongs to the Cuzco-Bolivia variety. Unfortunately, the literature describing Arequipa Quechua is very scant, indeed, and one must therefore rely for insight on the far more extensive analyses of the varieties spoken in Cuzco, Puno, and Bolivia.[fn 9] Quechua is an agglutinative language, with morphologically complex words constructed exclusively through suffixation. Each suffix usually consists of one or two syllables corresponding to a single morpheme, with word stress on the penultimate syllable." -- verbatim as reported (the reader's [..…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the (suffixed) word, so stress moves rightward as suffixes are added (e.g. maqa-wá-nki); word-final enclitics are therefore unstressed, except the 'speculative' enclitic -chá, which carries (final) stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Word-final 'Speculative' enclitic /-chá/ is stressed (final stress); the 1999 ILV La Unión writing guide (p. 14) likewise marks final stress with a tilde only on 'algunas enfáticas: hamuyyá, pichá, manamá, arí, mamáy, awiláy'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement (morphological word including suffixes); author's footnote 9 says the chapter is 'based on personal observation, as well as information gleaned from' published grammars of Cuzco, Puno and Bolivian Quechua, so the stress statement is first-hand for Chalhuanca (Caylloma, Arequipa) speech but phrased pan-Southern-Quechua; no instrumental data, no citation forms vs phrase distinction.
new_statements.identity_note: Courtney 1998 describes the Quechua of Chalhuanca (district Yanque, province Caylloma, dept. Arequipa), which she herself assigns to the 'Cuzco-Bolivia variety'; Glottolog files this thesis under areq1237 and SIL's archive files the Caylloma papers (Kindberg 1989) under qxu ('Highland/Northern Arequipa' dialects), but the core of qxu/areq1237 is La Unión province (Cotahuasi; Glottolog dialect cota1243), whose speech the 1987 ILV guide shows differs (La Unión puri-cha-ni vs Chivay/Caylloma puri-sha-ni, Cabanaconde puri-chha-ni) and which Glottolog classes as Ayacuchan. The only La Unión-specific items read (Buckingham 1992; ILV 1999 Runasimita Qillqasun p. 14) are consistent (tilde only on final-stressed emphatics) but do not state the default rule. If the catalog keys strictly to Cotahuasi/La Unión, treat Courtney as adjacent-dialect (Caylloma, arguably cusc1236) evidence.

new_statements.quote: In most Quechua dialects stress is assigned to the penultimate vowel of each polysyl- labic word form and thus provides an easy phonology-based criterion for word delimita- tion. Exceptionally, in interjections and emphatic expressions, stress can be word-final, e.g. in alalaw 'how cold!'. In Tarma and the dialect of northern Junin word-final stress can occur as a result of the elision of a final syllable. [p. 206] ... In Pacaraos Quechua (see section 3.2.9) stress is phonemic. It may lie either on the penultimate or on the final syllable. [...] Otherwise, penultimate stress is predominant. More complex, non-penultimate stress patterns, involving word-initial stress and stress dependent on syllable structure, are found in QI Ancash and in QI Cajatambo (cf. Torero 1964: 461; Parker 1976). [p. 207]
new_statements.citation: Adelaar, Willem F. H. & Pieter C. Muysken. 2004. The Languages of the Andes. Cambridge: CUP. pp. 183-188 (classification of Arequipa-La Unión), pp. 206ff (Quechua stress).
new_statements.locator: p. 206 (section 3.2.5 Phonology; page located by running-header probe '206 3 The Inca Sphere'), continued p. 207 ('The Quechuan language family 207'); dialect geography p. 187 (section 3.2.3 Dialect situation)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened and the 160+ raw snippet files it was chained from (dumped to one transcript); every sentence of the reported quote is there word for word (scanned hyphenation 'polysyl- labic', 'delimita- tion' kept). new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the existing Courtney 1998 statement (penultimate), but at the level of 'most Quechua dialects' rather than Arequipa-La Unión specifically; adds the emphatic/interjection final-stress exception, which matches the ILV 1999 Runasimita Qillqasun tilde-only-on-emphatic-final-stress note already; Identity: p. 187 puts the Arequipa provinces of Caravelí, Condesuyos and La Unión under Ayacucho Quechua and the provinces of Arequipa, Castilla, Caylloma and Condesuyos under Cuzco Quechua.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Family-wide statement: in most Quechua dialects stress falls on the penultimate vowel of every polysyllabic word, and this serves as a word-delimitation cue. The book gives no stress statement specific to Arequipa or La Unión Quechua; the named exceptions (phonemic final/penultimate contrast in Pacaraos, word-initial and weight-dependent patterns in quantity-insensitive Ancash and Cajatambo, final stress from syllable elision in Tarma and northern Junín) all concern Quechua I or Pacaraos, none the Arequipa varieties, which the book assigns to Quechua IIC (Ayacucho and Cuzco Quechua).
new_statements.exceptions: Interjections and emphatic expressions may carry word-final stress (alalaw 'how cold!'); word-final stress from elision of a final syllable in Tarma and northern Junín; Pacaraos has phonemic final vs penultimate stress (final stress with the first-person marker -'y and elided suffixes); quantity-insensitive Ancash and Cajatambo have word-initial and syllable-structure-dependent patterns; Huaraz stress pattern described by Torero 1964 in terms of long (CVC, CV:) vs short (CV) syllables; footnote 24: whether an Ancash-type accentuation reflects Proto-Quechua is debated.
new_statements.identity_note: Adelaar & Muysken 2004 p. 187 split the department of Arequipa between two Quechua IIC dialects: 'Ayacucho Quechua covers.. Arequipa (provinces of Caraveli, Condesuyos and La Union)' and 'Cuzco Quechua includes.. Arequipa (provinces of Arequipa, Castilla, Caylloma and Condesuyos)'. So the La Unión (Cotahuasi) part of Glottolog's areq1237 is Ayacucho-type and the Caylloma/Castilla part Cuzco-type in their scheme; Courtney 1998's field site (Chalhuanca, Caylloma) is on the Cuzco side. The book has no stress statement for either Arequipa variety; only the family-wide penultimate rule applies. They also note (p. 175) that the upper Colca basin (Caylloma) was once Aymara-speaking and is 'entirely Quechuanised today', and that glottalised/aspirated consonants in Cuzco, Puno, Arequipa and Bolivian Quechua are generally attributed to Aymaran diffusion.
